props.title: The Good Thief
props.initialSlug: Master thief plans one last heist in glamorous Nice

sections.content: **The Good Thief** (2002) stands as Neil Jordan's stylish reimagining of Jean-Pierre Melville's classic **Bob le Flambeur** (1956). Nick Nolte delivers a captivating performance as Bob, a heroin-addicted gambler planning an elaborate heist in the glittering underbelly of Nice. The film brilliantly updates the French New Wave's fascination with American noir, while adding modern touches like freeze-frames and jump cuts that pay homage to Jean-Luc Godard's **Breathless** (1960). Jordan's direction gives the French Riviera a neon-soaked darkness that recalls the atmospheric tension of **To Catch a Thief** (1955).

sections.content: The Good Thief sits within a rich tradition of European crime films that merge existential themes with heist mechanics. Like **Rififi** (1955) and **The Italian Job** (1969), it's as much about the psychology of the thief as the mechanics of the crime. Nolte's Bob shares DNA with other noble criminal protagonists like Robert De Niro's Neil McCauley in **Heat** (1995) - professional thieves with personal codes operating in morally ambiguous territory.

Jordan infuses the film with a jazzy, improvisational energy that recalls the French New Wave while incorporating more contemporary influences. The handheld camerawork and fragmented editing style shows the influence of Wong Kar-wai's **Chungking Express** (1994), while the neon-noir atmosphere draws from Michael Mann's **Thief** (1981). The film's exploration of addiction and redemption adds layers of complexity rarely seen in standard heist movies. SUBHEAD: Art and Authenticity in the Criminal Underworld

sections.content: A fascinating subplot involves art forgery and the theft of priceless paintings, connecting The Good Thief to films like **The Thomas Crown Affair** (1999) and **F for Fake** (1973) that explore the thin line between art and crime. The film's meditation on authenticity - in art, in personal relationships, in criminal enterprise - adds intellectual depth to its genre thrills. Like **Inside Man** (2006), it uses the heist format to explore larger questions about value and deception.
